title: India's ₹55,000-Crore Snack Industry Joins the Global Fibremaxxing Wave
excerpt: From millet cookies to fiber-fortified namkeens, Indian snack makers are racing to capitalise on the booming demand for gut-friendly, high-fiber products.
body:
• India's ₹55,000–60,000 crore snack market is pivoting toward fiber-fortified products as the global "fibremaxxing" trend gains ground.
  • ITC acquired Yoga Bar as a wholly-owned subsidiary in April 2026 and Marico picked up a 60% stake in Cosmix Wellness for ₹375 crore, signaling big-money bets on functional snacking.
  • Indian consumers now pay 22% more for healthier snack variants, with Gen Z driving demand for millet, ragi, and high-fiber options.
  • India's healthy snacks segment is projected to nearly double from US$4.4 billion in 2025 to US$8.2 billion by 2033.

A trend that started as social media shorthand for loading up on dietary fiber has turned into a full-blown commercial opportunity for India's snack industry. "Fibremaxxing" — the push to pack more fiber into everyday foods — is reshaping product lines from multinational FMCG giants to scrappy Indian startups.

From Hashtag to Factory Floor

The fibremaxxing movement went mainstream earlier this year when PepsiCo released a prebiotic soda and declared that "fibre will be the next protein." The underlying logic is straightforward: average global fiber consumption sits at around 18 grams per day, well short of the 25 to 38 grams recommended for adults. That gap represents what Barclays analyst Alex Sloane calls a "sizable structural runway" — a potential 7% compound annual growth rate in incremental fiber demand over five years.

In India, the math is even more compelling. The country's snack market is valued at ₹55,000–60,000 crore in 2026, spanning traditional namkeens, chips, extruded snacks, and bakery items. Within that, the healthy snacks segment generated US$4,419 million in revenue in 2025 and is on track to reach US$8,183 million by 2033, growing at 8.1% annually.

Big Players Are Betting Big

India's largest food conglomerates are moving fast. In April 2026, ITC brought Yoga Bar under its wing as a wholly-owned subsidiary, merging the brand's protein-bar lineup with ITC's distribution network of over 6 million retail outlets. ITC's broader Mission Millet initiative already spans Sunfeast Farmlite millet cookies — made from ragi and jowar with no added maida — alongside Aashirvaad multi-millet mixes, ragi flour, and gluten-free flour, all positioned as fiber-rich alternatives.

"With Mission Millet, we have embarked on a journey to build a culture of millet consumption through an exciting range of 'good-for-you' product portfolio."

— Ali Harris Shere, COO, Biscuits and Cakes Cluster, ITC Foods Division

Two months earlier, Marico acquired a 60% stake in Cosmix Wellness for ₹375 crore, targeting the premium wellness segment. Meanwhile, PepsiCo has reportedly expressed interest in a minority stake in Haldiram, India's ethnic-snack powerhouse with annual revenues exceeding ₹8,000 crore — a move that would bring fiber-fortification expertise to one of the country's most trusted traditional snack brands.

Startups Riding the Wave

It's not just legacy FMCG companies. New Delhi-based health-tech startup Fiberise Fit launched FYBER, a fiber-based weight management product developed with clinical inputs from AIIMS, New Delhi. The initial inventory — worth over ₹1 crore — sold out within hours of going live in March 2026. Fiberise has filed over 16 patents in functional nutrition and set an ambitious target of building a ₹10,000-crore brand within 1,000 days.

"Consumers are actively looking for safer and more scientific approaches to weight management."

— Professor Diwakar Vaish, Founder, Fiberise Fit

Why Indian Consumers Are Ready

The demand side backs up the supply-side frenzy. A Worldpanel by Numerator study found that Indian consumers are willing to pay 22% more for "healthy" variants of food products — and this isn't limited to affluent urban households. Even lower socio-economic groups (SEC D/E) pay 17% more for healthier options.

Gen Z is accelerating the shift. Around 70% of India's young consumers prefer frequent, smaller snack-based meals over traditional eating patterns, and they invest more time researching nutritional content than older generations. Social media functions as a primary source of food inspiration, pushing demand for baked, high-protein, plant-based, and fiber-rich variants including millet and quinoa snacks.

India's regulatory environment is also nudging the industry forward. FSSAI dietary guidelines now actively promote whole grain and millet consumption, and government-backed campaigns around millets as climate-smart superfoods — a push that gained global visibility during the 2023 International Year of Millets — continue to shape consumer expectations.

The Road Ahead

India currently accounts for 4.1% of the global healthy snacks market but is the fastest-growing regional market in Asia Pacific. Industry analysts project the broader Indian snacks market could double from ₹46,000 crore in 2024 to over ₹1,01,800 crore by 2033. The namkeen segment alone is expected to add US$4.89 billion in value by 2030, driven by retail expansion in Tier-II and Tier-III cities.

Whether the fibremaxxing trend becomes as durable as the protein craze depends on whether fortified products can clear the "health washing" bar — critics note that adding fiber to ultra-processed snacks doesn't make them genuinely healthy. But for now, the market signal is clear: India's snack industry is betting that fiber is the next frontier, and the money is following.
nri_angle: India's snack industry is embracing fiber-fortified products at a time when health-conscious NRIs are already seeking out millet and traditional snacks that align with the global fibremaxxing trend.
